CausalChain: Icaritin inhibits IL-6/JAK2/STAT3 signaling -> Reduced PD-L1 expression on HCC cells -> Decreased T cell exhaustion and enhanced CD8+ T cell activity -> Icaritin modulates ERα36 signaling -> Attenuation of oncogenic, epigenetic, and CSC-mediated immune evasion signals -> Synergizes with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade -> Enhanced anti-tumor immune response
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in HBV-associated HCC tumors characterized by high ERα36 and PD-L1, Icaritin treatment will reprogram the tumor microenvironment by concurrently reducing PD-L1 expression via inhibition of the IL-6/JAK2/STAT3 pathway and modulating ERα36-driven oncogenic as well as epigenetic signals. By employing state-of-the-art omics and genome editing methods, this dual modulation is predicted to counteract CSC-mediated immune evasion, reduce chronic inflammation, and promote enhanced CD8+ T cell-mediated antitumor immunity, thereby significantly improving the therapeutic efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors.
Abstract: In this study, we propose that in a well‐characterized subset of HBV-associated hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) with elevated ERα36 and PD-L1 expression, Icaritin treatment can reprogram the tumor microenvironment through a multi-pronged mechanism. Building on its established role in inhibiting the IL-6/JAK2/STAT3 pathway, Icaritin is hypothesized to reduce PD-L1 expression and modulate oncogenic signaling mediated by ERα36. Additionally, leveraging contemporary high-throughput omics, epigenetic profiling, and CRISPR-based perturbation techniques, we aim to demonstrate that Icaritin also reconfigures epigenetic regulators and cancer stem cell (CSC)-associated pathways. This integrated modulation is expected to mitigate chronic inflammation, diminish T cell exhaustion by enhancing CD8+ T cell function, and ultimately synergize with immune checkpoint inhibitors to elicit a robust anti-tumor immune response.
Orignal_vs_New: The revised hypothesis retains the original causal chain wherein Icaritin's inhibition of IL-6/JAK2/STAT3 signaling leads to reduced PD-L1 expression and its modulation of ERα36 signaling dampens oncogenic signals, ultimately enhancing the efficacy of PD-1/PD-L1 blockade. In response to reviewer feedback, we have expanded the mechanistic scope by incorporating the roles of epigenetic modifications and CSC-associated immune evasion, factors highlighted by recent observations of tumor heterogeneity and chronic inflammation. Additionally, we have integrated contemporary technological approaches (e.g., high-throughput omics and CRISPR-based assays) to enhance the practical investigability and the mechanistic validation of our proposed intervention.
